relevance_note: The paper describes three individual patients with GFAP variants: "We describe three patients with unique characteristics, and whose mutations have implications for AxD diagnosis".
method_note: Built with a Python script from my own reading of the paper; every span was checked by script to occur verbatim in the paper. Table 1 (3 rows) was read by hand. In scope: Patients 1-3; the mother of Patient 1 (tested negative); both parents of Patient 2 (blood DNA wild type) and both parents of Patient 3 (variant absent), whose sexes are not stated; the previously published Japanese patient of Murakami et al., 2008 (same c.1249delG, individual facts given in the Discussion); and another suspected AxD patient in whom GeneDx found 'the same mutation' as Patient 2 (label 'unnamed person 1'; variant recorded as Patient 2's c.1292_1299delinsATC with both spans). Out of scope: the father of Patient 1 (deceased, not tested, nothing else described); patients 5 and 10 of Brenner et al. (2001), used as RT-PCR controls, whose variants (R239C or R416W) are not attributed to either person; the 525 Ashkenazi Jewish controls. Relatives who tested negative have no variant rows. Patient 1's nucleotide change is described on NG_008401.1 (genomic) per the Table 1 note, so transcript_as_stated is 'not reported' for her; NM_002055.4 is given for the nucleotide changes of patients 2 and 3 and for all protein changes. Table 1 prints Patient 1's protein change as 'p.Glu207_Lys260del1' (footnote marker 1); the text form p.Glu207_Lys260del was used. Patient 1's age 39 is the age stated with her death ('was a 39 year old woman ... who died'), recorded as age at last evaluation; deceased_age left null because the age at death is not stated explicitly. Patient 1's ethnicity (Ashkenazi Jewish) comes from the ethnically matched control samples. Patient 1's normal cranial MRI at 29 excludes nothing more specific; cerebral white matter and medulla items are observed from autopsy neuropathology (myelin loss; medulla atrophy), not MRI. Visual evoked responses were normal at 29 and abnormal nine years later (change over time, both rows emitted). Patient 2: 'evaluated for developmental delay and intermittent ataxia' at 1 year vs 'not ataxic' at 33 months and 'no cerebellar deficits' - treated as a contradiction: both rows emitted, ataxia checklist item not reported. Patient 2's MRI checklist items (white matter, periventricular rim, basal ganglia/thalami, contrast enhancement) are excluded from 'meets none of these criteria'; the brain stem criterion does not cover the cervical cord, so the medulla item stays not reported. Ventriculomegaly was not treated as hydrocephalus. Patient 3: onset recorded as 'four months', the first age with symptoms; age at death 'just before one year of age' not converted; cause of death not stated explicitly. The periventricular rim item is excluded only from the 6-month MRI. The medulla item is observed from 'criterion 4 was met' near death plus the contrast with the Japanese child ('involvement of the pons and medulla was not described in the Japanese child'), an inference. 'No regression' was not used to exclude cognitive decline. Murakami patient: 'no reported feeding problems or GE reflux' and pons/medulla 'not described' were treated as not reported. Father of Patient 2: head circumference 61 cm, 'well above the 98%', recorded as macrocephaly observed. No stacked cells, no table symbols. No contradictions in variant data found.
